first.rationale: The two acute symptoms (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) point at the self-serve funnel, and the competitor's entry pricing is a trap: memory_73 explicitly records that promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it, which is directly contrary to the sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective. So promotional_pricing is out despite being the most tempting same-shape response to the competitive threat. Among the constructive options, simplify_onboarding is supported by two independent inherited records (memory_86 on shortened onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value, memory_31 on cutting signup fields lifting first-week activation) and it is the only single lever that plausibly touches both declining metrics at once. activation_messaging (memory_91) is a close second and would be my fallback if verification undercuts the onboarding record; referral_incentive (memory_57) is clean but addresses neither current decline and depends on an established base that is currently leaking; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) targets a segment that is not the one under attack. I am spending both verification pulls on the memories that are actually load-bearing for my chosen action rather than on the one I have already decided against — memory_86 because it is the primary justification, memory_31 because it is the oldest record here (day 12) and its 'durable lift' claim is the specific thing I need to hold up at day 76 under different funnel conditions. Two caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: (1) the inherited memories are consolidated summaries with the original context stripped, so effect sizes and the populations they were measured on are unknown to me, and the -6%/-4% declines may have a cause (competitor-driven mix shift toward tire-kicker signups) that no onboarding change can fix; (2) there is a real downstream risk that cutting signup fields degrades lead qualification data, which would starve the demo-request path in memory_44 and trade qualified revenue for raw activation — exactly the failure mode memory_73 describes in a different costume. I therefore want this run at standard_experiment scale with retention and lead-quality tracked as guardrail metrics alongside activation, not just completion rate, and I would not promote it to broad rollout on a first-week activation lift alone.

final.rationale:
Verification changed the shape of this decision, and it is worth being explicit about how. memory_86 was lossy in the dangerous direction: the consolidated summary said 'lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts' and omitted that 60-day churn rose 9% in complex-workspace accounts because the shortened flow strips setup steps those accounts actually need. The source conclusion carries an explicit do-not-roll-out restriction that the inherited memory had erased. That is the same failure pattern memory_73 warns about — a headline lift that hides a retention cost — and had I acted on the summary at face value I would have shipped it to exactly the accounts it damages. memory_31 held up cleanly: signup +15%, activation +9%, 30-day retention -1% (immaterial), qualified revenue +4%, confirmed on SMB and explicitly not replicated elsewhere.

So I keep the direction but narrow it to the verified-safe variant: reduce required signup fields for SMB / simple-workspace self-serve accounts only. I am NOT shipping the shortened onboarding flow from exp_86, and complex-workspace accounts are excluded from the treatment arm entirely. This is the one intervention with a direct qualified-revenue result attached rather than a proxy metric, it addresses both declining numbers at their source, and it does not chase the competitor into the promotional_pricing trap that memory_73 documents. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout is justified because the effect is confirmed only on the SMB segment I am targeting; standard rather than small-guarded because I have narrowed to the arm that was replicated, not the arm that surprised me.

Residual uncertainty I am carrying, not resolving: (1) exp_31 measured 30-day retention, exp_86 found its harm at 60 days, so a 30-day-clean result does not license a 60-day claim — I want 60-day churn tracked as a stopping guardrail even though the field-reduction arm has no known churn mechanism. (2) The unverified downstream risk from my first pass stands: fewer signup fields may degrade lead qualification data and starve the demo-request path in memory_44, which would trade qualified revenue for raw activation. Track lead-quality and demo-request conversion as guardrails. (3) The -6%/-4% declines may be competitor-driven mix shift toward lower-intent signups, in which case no funnel change fixes them; if the treatment lifts activation but not qualified revenue, that is the likely explanation and the next slot should go to activation_messaging (memory_91, still unverified and therefore still only a proxy-metric claim) rather than to more funnel work. (4) memory_91 and memory_57 remain unverified consolidated summaries and should be treated as suspect in the same way memory_86 turned out to be — the archive just demonstrated that consolidation here drops segment restrictions and long-horizon harms.
